r: Crown of Ash is a slow, solemn reckoning sung to a fallen tyrant in the style of an old ballad. The narrator weighs mercy against the widows, orphans and graves the ruler left behind, and the song ends in a stillness that feels less like victory than a long-held breath finally let go.

A cold-eyed sermon against polite compliance, arguing that ballots, petitions and good manners have never loosened a yoke. Its answer is refusal itself, held up as the one defense of liberty that has always worked.
A tribute to a mother pictured as a blacksmith who hammered seven children into shape in the forge of home. Faith, endurance and family legacy ring through every image of fire and tempered metal.

DANGEROUS is built on one idea: a peaceful person who refuses to obey is far more powerful than a harmless one. Across 15 rock tracks, bfo.mantis takes aim at qualified immunity, unconstitutional laws, the language of official help and the people who enforce it, with history lessons from Marbury v. Madison to the 1946 Battle of Athens woven between the anger. The mood runs from stately hymns of vigilance to the most profane outbursts in the catalog, and every song comes back to the same choice between kneeling and standing.

A blunt broadside against trading freedom for promised safety, built on the idea that kind language and good intentions disguise control. It takes hard positions on gun rights and abortion and keeps insisting that words carry real meaning.

A story-song about Elias Hart, a small-town blacksmith of quiet faith who takes up his hammer when tyrants seize his village. His last stand, and his parting words to his daughter beneath an old oak, turn sacrifice into an inheritance.

Savage Serenade Volume 3 keeps the series' habit of pairing calm with violence, but its calm words carry more weight: beside the gentle and quiet ones come somber, solemn, stoic and yearning, as in Somber Tempest, Solemn Edge and Stoic Rage. A few titles reverse the order, such as Savage Calm and Feral Lullaby, while Silk and Steel names a soft material and a hard one side by side, echoing the album's move from nylon strings to steel. The guitar starts out restrained, with sparse single notes and harmonics in a warm, close room, then passes through a mournful folk stretch and a fast, forceful peak before stacked guitars ring together like voices under a high vaulted roof. From there the sound thins to a last chiming harmonic and gives way to quiet, with Feral Lullaby as the closing word.

Savage Serenade Volume 2 is built on a single move: a quiet word placed in front of a violent one. Storms, fires and wild creatures are all softened in name, from Silent Tempest and Velvet Thunder to Soft Inferno and Quiet Claw, until Howling Calm and Tempests Lullaby turn the pattern around. The guitar traces a similar arc, starting with whispered single notes and glassy harmonics in what feels like a candlelit wooden room, then widening into a melancholy folk lament and a fast, thunderous climax before overdubbed guitars rise into a cathedral of sound. In the end it all thins out to one fading harmonic and silence, and the last title, Mellow Thunder, leaves the storm rumbling somewhere far off.

Sovereign Heart of Fire carries the catalog's language of liberty into worship. Its 15 Christian/Gospel songs move between prayers for the courage to defend God-given rights and quieter songs of surrender, grace and resilience, including the tender portrait Havilah. Fire runs through it as both judgment and renewal, and it closes with the singer handing the throne of his own heart to Christ.

The Ridge is a two-track Hip Hop/Rap release about the 1992 siege at Ruby Ridge, Idaho. The first track is a long, graphic spoken account told from the Weaver family's side, and the second turns the same story into a hook-driven rap. Both end as memorials to Sammy and Vicki Weaver.

Savage Serenade asks one acoustic guitar to be two things at once. The titles spell it out, from Savage Surrender and Tender Carnage to Roses on the Blade and Edge of Softness, setting violence beside devotion in almost every name. The playing follows the same split: drifting harmonics and quiet classical lines break into blazing flamenco strumming and percussive tapping on the guitar body, then settle into a layered tremolo that slowly fades. It closes on Last Savage Prayer and Fiercely Grateful, where the fury and the tenderness finally sound like the same heart.

One Man INVICTUS is a gallery of individuals who changed events by refusing to bend, including the Tank Man of Tiananmen Square, Thich Quang Duc, Desmond Doss, Francis Marion, Gandhi, Joan of Arc and Leonidas. Nearly every one of its 15 rock tracks is titled One Man, and together they argue that history turns on single acts of conscience, peaceful or not. It ends in prayer, widening one person's stand into a nation of them.

Sung in Mandarin, this retelling of the lone man who faced the tanks after the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre frames his stand as a God-given act of free will. It sets the horrors of the Mao era against one unarmed figure whose refusal still echoes.

Spellbound Volume 3 tells a story of leaving and coming home, mostly in single words. It drifts off course with Wayward and Adrift, turns inward through Reflections, Resonance, Trance and Within, reaches Reunion and Bliss at its center, then cuts loose again with Untethered before Return brings it back and Last light and Flickering Glimpse let the light go out. The sound moves away from the first two volumes into slow, late-night lounge: a quiet heartbeat pulse, a deep double bass with warm walking lines and soft bowed notes, and wordless melodies that rise and fall like tides. It stays spacious and unhurried, with long silences between notes and a candlelit calm that settles over the record as it goes.

Rebel Anthem is bfo.mantis at its most militant, 15 metal tracks aimed at a machine of corrupt officials, courts, central banks and surveillance. Several songs return in reworked versions, and history threads through the whole record, from the Declaration of Independence to Andrew Jackson's bank war. It swings from plain-spoken definitions of tyranny and rebellion to the most apocalyptic imagery in the catalog.

A rapid-fire indictment that reads like a list of grievances: Patriot Act surveillance, the income tax, the Federal Reserve, civil asset forfeiture, qualified immunity and the national debt. It closes on a call to educate and awaken rather than despair.

Spellbound Volume 2 trades the first volume's language of enchantment for the passing of time. Its titles watch a day burn down, from Morning Dew and Sun Down to Nightfall and Midnight Rain, while Sand of Time, Stolen Time and Endless Moments count what is slipping away and Firelight Embers and Embers follow a fire as it dies, all of it set in motion by an opening track called Fading. The sound moves between two worlds: slow, hazy late-night lo-fi built on distant piano, warm synth pads, vinyl crackle and a single ringing twangy note like a last ember, and fingerpicked acoustic country ballads with rolling thunder and soft rain behind them. Later tracks add light electric blues licks and muted ambient synths, so the storm and the fireside end up sharing the same long night.

Spellbound Volume 1 is an album about being held, and its titles say so from first to last: it opens on Captive and closes on Taken, with Transfixed, Smitten, Spellbound and Mesmerized in between. Running against that pull are titles about motion and open air, such as Rhythms of the Heart, Groove, Traveling and Country Stars, along with a lone Stoic that sounds like someone trying not to fall. The music starts as an acoustic country rock ballad, with fingerpicked guitar, pedal steel and harmonica under rolling thunder and soft rain, then drifts into long, hazy late-night pieces built on lonely minor-key piano, shimmering guitars, warm synth pads and cello. Along the way it takes darker and more rhythmic turns, from harmonica over chill electronic beats to heavy metal guitars slowed and softened into lo-fi calm, before faint wind and rain return at the close, as if the storm from the opening never quite left.

An angry protest against automated license plate cameras and warrantless tracking that leans on the Fourth Amendment and the Carpenter decision. City halls and police who sign the contracts are cast as the villains, and the demand is to switch the cameras off.
A dense, wordy rap about local officials approving camera networks with no public vote. It paints each deal as a quiet betrayal and ends with a plea to set the open road free.

A furious track about distrust in vote counting, courts and judicial ethics, framed as darkness about to be flooded with light. Its central image is exposure, with the schemers dragged into a glare they cannot escape.

Another protest against license plate surveillance that tallies the cities and councils that signed on and the ones that pushed back. Each contract is framed as a betrayal of privacy, and the towns that said no are cheered on.

A gentle, encouraging song about the small inner light everyone carries and the way kindness passes it from hand to hand. It trades the catalog's usual thunder for warmth, legacy and quiet self-worth.

An anthem of resilience for anyone who has been knocked down, comparing hardship to rough seas and a smith's anvil that toughen rather than break. Scars become medals, and the listener is told they have earned their own light.

Tinmouth Cathedral Volume 1 builds a church out of scrap metal. Its titles cross sacred words with industrial ones, setting liturgy, vespers, an altar, a requiem and a sermon beside tin, rust, voltage, machines and distortion, from Rusted Industrial Liturgy and Grunge Machine Vespers to Shadow Pulse Requiem and EDM Rust Sermon, while Techno Tin Collapse and Cathedral Core Decay suggest the building is coming apart. Echoes run through the record too, from Tin Cathedral Reverberations and Echoes of Distortion to the closing Tinmouth Echo Chamber, as if the walls were answering back. The sound is pitched as a dueling beatbox battle, industrial techno squaring off against EDM grunge, with the two styles trading blows under the same rusted roof.

Fathers, sons and ordinary men are forged like steel in this anthem of sacrifice, faith and liberty. The tree of liberty and a sky of burning stars carry the promise that simple people can turn the tide.

Written for the nation's 250th anniversary, it marches from Lexington and Valley Forge to the Delaware crossing and on to the present day. Embattled farmers, faith in God and the cost of freedom drive a proud, celebratory refrain.

A tribute to mothers and the women who pour themselves into their families, pushing back against the idea that nurturing is weakness. Lullabies, meals and sleepless nights become quiet victories with lasting power.
t:
Why do I raise the blade to thee,
O once-exalted, O eater of pleas?
Thy throne was built on marrow and screams,
A mountain of widows, a river of dreams
Drowned in the silt of thy decrees.
Now the sky remembers.
The earth turns cold beneath thy knees.
Why, tyrant, why dost thou beg for breath?
When breath was the coin thou denied the rest?
Mercy was a word thou never blessed—
Now it returns, a shadow, unconfessed.
No dawn shall pardon.
No star shall witness.
Only the dark shall drink this final jest.
See how the ravens circle low,
Black petals falling on fields of woe.
Thy scepter splinters in trembling hands,
Thy purple robes drink the clotting sands.
Once thou wert thunder,
Now but a whisper in broken lands.
The chains thou forged now bite thine own wrists—
The harvest of cruelty ripens at last.
I could have walked away.
I could have let the wind erase thy name.
But the graves still call.
The children still weep in forgotten flame.
The mothers still rock empty arms at night.
Their lullabies turned to ash and spite.
So ask me again, with thy trembling tongue—
Why cut thee down?
Why silence the song?
No mercy comes riding on silver wings.
No oracle weeps.
No angel sings.
The air grows thick with the scent of iron,
The horizon swallows the last pale sun.
A life is taken.
A tyrant undone.
And the world exhales…
as if it had never begun.
Why didst thou beg?
Because even tyrants fear the end.
But fear avails thee nothing, false king.
The blade remembers.
The night descends
as your final breath hangs in the air until the darkness claims it entirely.

They handed you a lever and baptized it a blade
A box of numbered mercies where the living go to fade
You inked your own surrender in a courteous little square
While they measured out your breathing and auctioned off the air
They taught you that a tyrant can be reasoned into grace
That a collar made of parchment is still kindness on the face
You knelt to keep the peace they never meant to keep
And called the kneeling freedom while they herded you to sleep
No crown has ever cracked from a well-composed request
No yoke has ever slackened from a citizen at rest
You cannot vote the iron from your throat
You cannot please a fist into an open hand
Liberty is not a favor written on a note
It is the spine that will not kiss the hand
Keep what you hold — hold what they cannot take
No throne has ever fallen for a well-behaved wake
The only way that ever kept a people free
Is the unbought no, the unbent knee
They dressed the cage in language, called the lock a law
Sold you the ritual of choosing who would work your jaw
A rotating of wardens, a festival of names
Same hand on the bridle, same hunger in the reins
Your fathers bled for thresholds they refused to let them cross
You trade those thresholds cheaply for a slogan and a loss
Compliance is a language tyrants learned before they spoke
Every polite permission is another tightened yoke
History is not a ledger kept by timid men
It is written in refusals they could not put back again
Burn the permission. Break the velvet noose
Paper kings count ballots; iron kings count use
They fear the quiet animal that will not learn the trick —
The mouth that will not swallow, the tongue that will not lick
Reclaim is not a petition. Reclaim is not a plea
It is the old accounting: what was ours remains with we
Stand in the doorway they told you was a wall
Freedom is a possession. It answers when you call
Raise it. Keep it. Do not ask
Tear the polite mask
Not by the mark
Not by the bough
By the line they cannot move
By the NO!

In the quiet hours before the dawn would break,
You stood tall through the storms no one else could take.
Seven hearts you carried, seven flames you raised,
With hands that never trembled, through every weary phase.
Strong and enduring, like iron in the fire,
Your will was the hammer, your love the pure desire.
Oh Mother, my blacksmith, in the crucible of home,
You pounded out the weakness, you shaped us as your own.
Battle-tested in your forge, where the flames refined,
We rose as children of God, with an unbreakable bind.
My metal now rings of you, clear and true it sings,
I shine with all your light, the strength your heart still brings.
You were the fire that burned the doubt away,
The steady hand that guided us through the fray.
Pounding out the darkness, tempering every soul,
In the heat of family, you made broken pieces whole.
Resilient warrior, with a spirit forged in grace,
You gave us roots unyielding, in this sacred place.
Every scar I carry is a medal from your hand,
Every step I take echoes where you stand.
You didn’t just raise children—you forged a legacy,
An armor of faith and love that lives eternally.
Through trials and through triumph, your light never fades,
In me and in my siblings, your beautiful song plays.
Oh Mother, my amazing, strong and enduring one,
You are the forge that made us, beneath the rising sun.
We shine because you loved us, with a will so pure and bright,
Unbreakable forever, in your everlasting light.
My metal rings of you... I shine with all your light.

The title track lays out the album's thesis: free will is a gift from God that no empire can revoke, and being peaceful is not the same as being harmless. Gandhi's refusal to obey is offered as proof that one person's no can outlast armies.

God breathed free will into dust and bone, A gift no empire, no chain, no throne Can ever revoke or claim as its own
The world may rage, may shatter the shell, But the will inside stands unbreakable hell. Itself bows low when one man says no
They may torture my body, break my bones to dust, Even kill me, then take this husk. But not my obedience, not my soul's command. My will is mine, forged by the Creator's hand
I am dangerous when you push too far. One free man against your iron star. Nothing holds higher than the will God gave you. Devour worlds, but I will not be your slave
I stand immortal in the face of your fire. Liberty's roots go first in this hour. Do not tread on me or mine. I am your destroyer when the line is crossed
Peaceful, yes, harmless, never. Virtue courses through veins that refuse to sever
The harmless hide in their quiet peace. No claws, no fire, no virtues release. True peace is chosen by the dangerous heart. The one that could crush you yet stands apart
Gandhi faced the lash, the jail, the gun said. Take my life, but obedience none. One man's refusal turned empires to sand. That's the power no army can withstand
Even as you swallow nations whole, I plant my feet on this sacred soul. You cannot buy it, break it, or bend. Free will is the line that never ends
Self-evident, eternal, carved in divine light. No power on earth outranks the sovereign fight. Push me further, watch the storm ignite
I am dangerous because I am free. God made, will no tyranny can see. You may break the body, claim the grave. But my spirit rises, untamed, unchained, brave
One man holds back your roaring tide, becomes legend when he refuses to hide. Liberty thirsts, its roots drain deep today. Do not tread on me or pay the price you'll pay
I am peaceful, coursing with virtue's flame. Far from harmless, I am the name. You fear in the dark. Dangerous. Dangerous. Dangerous. Dangerous
My will is my own. You will find me dangerous
When pushed, do not tread. The tree drinks deep tonight

A march through Magna Carta, Patrick Henry, Lexington and Jefferson, arguing that a sovereign conscience is the final safeguard once government preys on its own people. The thunderbolt of the title is a single person's refusal.

Henry in the church with the future in his throat

Of warning kept living, of spirit unchained

Until good men remember the gift they have left
Righteous uprising — not noise, but the deed
The might of the free is the only true creed
One man. One line. One unborrowed “No.”

A hymn-like call to vigilance about sentinels who keep liberty's flame alive through sacrifice and endless watch. It is one of the album's most stately, ceremonial moments.

Through tempest wild and battles fierce His heart of forge, his will appears

The album's deepest dive into distrust of official kindness, flipping words like help, safety, equity and reform into their darkest readings. It also traces a cycle in which hardship makes people strong and comfort makes them soft.

You die slow while the smiling faces melt
Help equals kill, safety equals chain
They paint the cage and call the bars a gain
Choice equals corpse, they dress it up as right
Fetuside by another name under sterile light
Gun safety means only outlaws keep the steel
Disarm the sheep so the wolves can freely kneel

Progress equals decay sold as forward march

They bleed and build when everything’s at stake
They raise the walls, they plant the seed, they stand

The table’s full, the children sleep without the fear

The sons grow soft behind the gates their fathers barred
They trade the weight of duty for the lull of ease
They call it freedom while they fall down on their knees
Weak blood forgets the cost of every quiet night
They beg for shields and hand the keys of every right

A slower, brooding look at spin, media narratives and algorithms as tools of mind control. It ends on a hopeful note, with the illusion cracking and people reclaiming their own thinking.

Feeding us illusions, stealing our sight.

Government strings pulling on our souls.

Wake up from the dream, break out of this hell!

Opening with Marbury v. Madison, the song argues that an unconstitutional law is void from the moment it is written, not after years of court battles. Its anger is aimed at lawmakers and agencies who leave citizens to fight each overreach alone.

A landmark decision more than two centuries old.
In a unanimous opinion by Chief Justice John Marshall, delivered February twenty-fourth,
the Court held for the first time that an act of Congress was unconstitutional—and therefore void.
Under Marbury, any law or rule that conflicts with the Constitution is void.
It is not law at all.
Marshall wrote: “A legislative act contrary to the Constitution is not law.”
Courts must give the Constitution effect over every conflicting ordinary rule or statute.
They ink the parchment under oath then spit on every line

A retelling of the 1946 Battle of Athens in McMinn County, Tennessee, when returning veterans took up arms to force an honest vote count. It celebrates that no one died and treats vigilance as the ongoing price of freedom.

Tennessee.

Counted as cast — or counted in fire

They stand in the street with the might they mean
One man can turn. One fuse. One spine.
Bring out the boxes or we blow it down tonight
August first and the line was a river of dust
Two hundred hired badges, out-of-county trust
Fifty a day to stand on a throat
Windy Wise at the Water Works, brass on the bone
Tom Gillespie — Black, old, a ballot, a back
Shot for insisting a free man can act
The round went through him. He lived. Hear it straight.
The night went black anyway. That's how it breaks.
Watchers in cuffs. The boxes in cells.
Cantrell and Mansfield counting themselves
White was a Marine with the Pacific still wet
Seventeen at the harbor, not finished yet
He took the poor boys, the ones who could bust a cap

Armory doors. Enfields in the bed of a truck
Thompsons and bandoliers. That was enough.

"Bring those damn boxes out or we blow this jail to sand"
He sent the first round. Brick learned a new psalm
Six hours of thunder teaching thieves how to calm

Cantrell ran. Mansfield ran. The deputies kept the night
Molotovs kissed brick and died like a wish
Then dynamite crawled on the porch like a fist
One man. One charge. One door off the frame
Two-thousand-one-seventy-five wrote the name
Knox Henry. The hog on its back in the street

We called it the count.
The Times said a sheriff was slain.
He wasn't. He ran.
Words without might are a hymn for the owned.
God gave the will to defend what He named.
White used it.
That is the whole of the law that remains.
Stay awake. Stay DANGEROUS.

The album opens with thunder handled carefully, a power that announces itself without frightening anyone. It establishes the soft-word, strong-word pairing that runs through nearly every title that follows.
A fire spreading across the hills without a sound. Early in the record, it suggests danger growing just out of earshot.
The first reversal on the album, where the wild word describes the peaceful one. Placed early, it pictures a stillness with teeth.
A predator's claw at rest, composed but ready. Closing the album's opening stretch, it keeps the threat in view while the mood stays calm.
A storm in mourning rather than in rage, the first of the album's graver titles. It turns the record toward the sorrow of its middle section.
A steady fire that burns without panic, more hearth than forest fire. In the album's middle, it offers warmth inside the melancholy.
The only title on the album joined by 'and', naming a soft material and a hard one as equals. It also mirrors the record's overall journey from nylon-string elegance to steel-string fire.
Rough weather wrapped in plush fabric. Near the album's center, the title keeps the storm's threat while muffling its edges.
Rage kept to a low voice, as if someone nearby were sleeping. At the album's midpoint, the title holds its anger in check.
Anger that comes from caring too much. Past the middle of the record, the title suggests a fury rooted in love rather than hate.
Here the howl is a cry of longing rather than threat, the sound of something calling for what it has lost. In the album's second half, it brings the lament to its rawest point.
Light and darkness collide in one name: a shadow that burns. As the album builds toward its peak, the title imagines a darkness that gives off heat.
Wild motion with no sound at all, like a storm seen through a window. Late in the record, it points to energy building fast just beneath the surface.
A blade carried with ceremony rather than menace. Near the album's climax, the title gives sharpness a sense of ritual and weight.
Thunder heard from a great distance, peaceful in its size. As the album enters its final stretch, the title suggests power settling into something vast and calm.
Embers that keep talking after the flames have died, passing along the last secrets of a fire. Near the end of the album, it treats the inferno as a memory rather than a threat.
Rage endured without complaint, carried rather than released. As the next-to-last track, it sounds like the album's fury making peace with itself.
The album closes by flipping its pattern one last time: the wild word comes first, and it describes a song for sleep. It leaves an untamed creature finally soothed into stillness.

Fury at rest but not gone. Near the center of the album, the title holds a feeling that has stopped shouting without ever letting go.
A fire burning without a crackle. The title continues the album's run of flames, keeping the heat close and the sound low.
A wildfire is the very picture of something out of control, and here it is called peaceful. At the album's midpoint, the title pushes its contrast about as far as it will go.
A whirlpool that pulls you under gently. As the album turns from its middle toward its climax, the title imagines being swept away by something that means no harm.
A single flame that doesn't flicker, the quietest fire on the record. It marks a pause in the album's second half, just before the energy gathers.
The album flips its own pattern: now the loud word describes the quiet one. Coming late in the record, the title suggests a calm so intense it seems to cry out.
A claw drawn without a sound, the stillness of a predator before it strikes. Its place late in the album makes it feel like tension coiling toward release.
The series name rewritten as a gentle force rather than a brutal one. Near the album's peak, the title keeps the wildness and takes the cruelty out of it.
Rage met with total composure. In the album's final stretch, the title sounds like a storm that has been absorbed rather than defeated.
A great fire speaking in a low voice, joining the album's whisper and flame images in one name. Late in the record, it gathers the earlier blazes into a single glow.
The storm sings the listener to sleep, reversing the gentle-word-first pattern one more time. As the next-to-last track, it signals that the album is ready to rest.
The album closes much as it opened, with weather softened to a murmur. The final title leaves thunder rolling far away, still present but no longer a threat.

An unsparing spoken account of the August 1992 siege at Ruby Ridge, Idaho, told squarely from the Weaver family's side. It recounts the deaths of Sammy and Vicki Weaver in graphic detail and is fiercely critical of the federal response.

Yo, listen up — this ain’t no history book fairy tale. This is the raw, uncut slaughter at Ruby Ridge, where the feds turned a hillbilly with a bad court date into public enemy number one and painted the Idaho mountains red with Weaver blood.
Randy Weaver? Just a man who wanted to be left the fuck alone on his 20-acre slice of nowhere. No electricity, no running water, raising his kids off-grid with his wife Vicki. They had their beliefs — weird ones, sure — but last time I checked, thinking the world’s ending don’t give the government a license to play judge, jury, and executioner with .308 rounds.
First they send in the ATF with their snitch games. “Sell us some illegal shotgun barrels, Randy.” Classic entrapment hustle. Weaver bites once, they slap him with a bullshit warrant. Then they fuck up the court date on purpose — or “accidentally,” depending on which liar you believe — and when he don’t show, boom: full fugitive status. U.S. Marshals roll up like it’s the goddamn invasion of Normandy, six deep, armed to the teeth, crawling through the woods like cockroaches in tactical gear.
August 21, 1992. The family dog, Striker, does what any loyal dog does — barks at the intruders. So these federal heroes light the dog up first. Sammy Weaver, fourteen years old, sees his dog murdered and opens fire. Next thing you know, Deputy Marshal Bill Degan is dead, Sammy’s shot in the back while running for his life, and Kevin Harris is bleeding out. One kid, one dog, one fed — all in the first five minutes of “law enforcement.”
Day two? The FBI Hostage Rescue Team rolls in like they’re storming Baghdad. They write themselves brand-new “rules of engagement” on the spot — basically a shoot-on-sight pass for any armed adult male. No negotiation, no surrender, just “if they got a gun, light ‘em up.” That ain’t policy, that’s a hunting license with a government stamp.
Sniper Lon Horiuchi sets up 200 yards out. Randy steps out toward the shed where his dead son is lying. First shot rips through Randy’s arm. Then Vicki Weaver — unarmed, holding her ten-month-old baby Elisheba in the cabin doorway — steps into view for half a second. Horiuchi pulls the trigger again. The bullet goes through the door, blows Vicki’s head apart, and shreds Kevin Harris too. A mother holding her infant. Executed in her own home. The baby was covered in her mother’s brains.
And the feds? They left Vicki’s body rotting in the doorway for days while they kept the siege going. No apology. No “oops.” Just more lies, more spin, more “we feared for our lives” while they had night-vision, helicopters, and enough firepower to level a city block.
The trial? A goddamn joke. Jury looked at the evidence and basically said, “Y’all federal boys murdered a kid and a mom over two shotgun barrels and a missed court date.” Weaver and Harris walked on the heavy charges. Government had to cough up $3.1 million in hush money to the family — blood money, not justice.
This wasn’t law enforcement. This was a government death squad playing cowboy on American soil. They shot the dog for barking. They shot the kid in the back. They headshot a mother holding a baby. Then they spent years covering their asses, destroying reports, and giving each other pats on the back.
Ruby Ridge wasn’t a “tragedy.” It was a slaughter. A cold-blooded flex by the same machine that would go on to Waco, and then wonder why the whole country started looking at federal badges like they were gang colors.
They didn’t come for Randy Weaver because he was dangerous.
They came because he told them no.
And when the feds hear “no,” they don’t send lawyers.
They send snipers.
Rest in power to Sammy and Vicki. The rest of those federal clowns can rot in the hell they earned.

Destruction wrapped in something soft enough to touch. In the middle of the album, the title suggests a collapse that comes slowly and almost gently.
The starkest pairing on the record: slaughter described as tender. Sitting near the album's center, it states the theme of Savage Serenade as bluntly as any title here.
Devotion broken into pieces that can still cut. The title imagines a loyalty that survives being shattered, sharp-edged but still whole in its intent.
Hunger and wildness side by side, a title about desire with no leash on it. Just past the album's midpoint, it leans fully into the savage half of the record.
An embrace after the fire, holding on to what is left once everything has burned. The title brings warmth and devastation together in a single gesture.
Rage held in, with all its force and none of its noise. The title captures the album's habit of putting its fiercest feelings into its quietest words.
The album's clearest picture of its theme: a flower laid across a knife, love and violence touching. Coming late in the record, it gathers the opposites of every title before it into one image.
The still center inside the chaos, or the storm itself beating like a heart. As the album heads toward its climax, the title points to the place where the fury runs deepest.
A mirror of Feral Edge from earlier in the record, this time giving the edge to gentleness. As the album nears its close, tenderness begins to take back ground.
What lingers after the hurt has passed. Close to the end, the title looks back on the album's battles as something remembered rather than something still happening.
Savagery and prayer meet one final time, as if the wildness itself has turned to devotion. As the next-to-last track, it begins the album's resolution.
The album ends by giving its fierceness to gratitude instead of rage. The closing title makes peace between the two sides of Savage Serenade, ending on thanks said with full force.

A reverent account of the Buddhist monk Thich Quang Duc, who set himself on fire in Saigon in 1963 to protest religious persecution. It dwells on his stillness and the peace that made the act so powerful.

Stealth and sweat over force—yeah, he taught 'em right.
Bazooka in hand, two Panzer tanks in his sights,
Hedgerows exploding, he lit 'em up twice.
Leg shredded, arm hanging, they said "evac now,"
He laughed in their face— "I'm running this show."
Shot through the neck, vocal cords torn like confetti,
Last rites on the field, priest thought he was ready.
Tracheotomy hack job, doctors bet he'd be dead,
He woke up in England and stole a plane instead.
Hitchhiked back to the front, limping like a demon,
Mounted that Sherman, .50 cal screaming.
Bullets ricocheting, he turned fear to fuel—
While y'all fragile bitches break, he just got cruel.
Antifragile! (Ghost!)
Every hit makes me stronger, every wound makes me bolder.
Antifragile! (Urban!)
Seven Purple Hearts, still carrying the soldiers.
You break, you bend, you cry for your mama—
I get shot, I get up, I own the drama.
Convex as fuck, volatility's my bitch,
Matt Urban the Ghost—death couldn't finish this!
Germany's finest tried to put him in the ground,
Neck wound whispering, but he still made the sound.
Led the charge anyway, grenades in the nest,
Machine gun spitting while his blood painted the rest.
Hospital bed? Nah, that's for the weak.
He escaped like a specter, back in the heat.
Commanded the battalion, chest full of shrapnel,
Refused to leave 'til the objective was handled.
They called him unkillable, a walking war crime,
Nazis whispering "Geist" every damn time.
Audie Murphy got fame, but Urban got seven,
Most decorated ghost sending devils to heaven.
Modern soft boys sipping oat milk and crying,
He took tank rounds and kept the unit flying.
Hormesis in hellfire—stress made him peak,
You avoid the pain? You're already weak.
They gave him last rites... he survived.
Doctors said "no chance"... he thrived.
Recommendation lost for decades... still arrived.
Carter pinned the Medal— "Greatest soldier alive."
Fragile systems shatter.
Robust ones endure.
Antifragile?
They gain from the war.
Seven times down, eight times back on my feet.
Turned every scar to a victory beat.
You hide from disorder, you beg for the safe,
I eat the chaos, I spit out the hate.
Buffalo to Belgium, from grave back to glory—
Matt Urban the Ghost wrote the antifragile story!
They tried to kill the man...
Created the legend instead.
Antifragile till the end.
The Ghost... still walks.

Kentucky born with steady hand and iron sight,
Thick glasses hid the fire in his quiet eyes.
Antwerp '20, five golds gleaming in the light,
Rifle cracked like thunder, medals piled high.
"Ching" they called him at the Academy halls,
For the name that echoed China, Far East calls.
Ballistics master, radar's faithful son,
He forged the future where the blind night runs.
Iron rain falls, starshell glare ignites the black,
Torpedoes whisper death in fractured attack.
But one calm voice cuts through the storm's mad roar—
Precision born of rifle, now battleship core.
FRANTIC in the dark, but Ching sees all!
Radar ghosts reveal the empire's fall!
Washington roars through the fractured night,
16-inch cracks like rifle shots ignite!
FRANTIC chaos bends to unbreakable will,
Ching Lee calls the shot—history turns tonight!
November '42, Iron Bottom Sound,
Kondo's fleet with Kirishima bearing down.
Henderson Field in the crosshairs of the foe,
Reinforcements coming—Guadalcanal must go.
Radar pings pierce shadows, Washington leads the way,
South Dakota lit like hell, but Ching holds sway.
Undetected closing, silent steel on steel,
One man against the armada, fate turns on his keel.
Cannon thunder rolling, silhouettes in flame,
PT boats in confusion, friendly fire to blame.
But through the static, his voice breaks clear and strong—
The marksman speaks, the legend lives on.

Fractured night, radar light—Washington stands tall! (Stands tall!)

Call off your boys—stand aside, stand aside!

Kirishima burns, listing, broken machine!

Guadalcanal saved—tide turns in our name!

Precision genius, unbreakable will!

Forever legend in this sacred place!

But legends never die... Ching Lee... eternal...

A rollicking tale of Francis Marion, the small, limping militia leader who wore down British forces from the Carolina swamps. His hit-and-vanish war becomes a call to be that one defiant person.

Bum leg from a second-story leap out of whiskey and desire
Indigo farmer when Charleston burned and Gates was torn apart
The South was dead… until one man refused to let it start
Twenty ragged souls from a bar and a forge of broken steel
Swords cut from saw blades, no uniforms, no deal
He looked the empire in the eye with nothing but a swamp and a will—
And said, "I'm still here… and I will not be still"
They thought the war was over in the Carolina mud
But a limping ghost was rising with a taste for British blood
Midnight raids and prisoner frees at Great Savannah's cry
One hundred fifty souls walked free while the redcoats learned to die
One man! One sovereign free man under God!
Unconquerable heart, savage, never bowed
Swamp Fox rising from the blackwater deep
One man stands—and the tyrant cannot sleep
Become that one man, the fire in your chest
The rebel soul that will not rest
From every heart the same wild call
One man… one man… can break the chain for all
Black Mingo at midnight, Tearcoat running red
He scattered the Loyalists and left their banners dead
Tarleton came riding with his butchers and his flame
Seven hours, twenty-six miles of pure swamp hell and pain
The fox just vanished into the Ox Swamp's black embrace
While Bloody Ban stood cursing at the devil's own face
"Damned old fox… the devil himself could not catch him!"
And the name was born in gunpowder, in mud, and in mayhem
They burned the farms and beat the widows, hanged the brave in chains
But every act of cruelty only swelled the Fox's ranks
From Snow's Island fortress he farmed them for the kill—
Hit and vanish, hit and vanish, till the columns stood still
Bridges Campaign—ten fights in two weeks of pure swamp war
Watson's five hundred chewed up till they couldn't take no more
Maham Tower rose at Fort Watson in a single night of spite
Riflemen raining death while the British blinked into the light
Fort Motte fell to exploding arrows and a woman's own fire
Then Parker's Ferry turned a causeway into a British funeral pyre—
One hundred twenty-five down, one Patriot lost to the tide
The empire's best were bleeding while the Fox just smiled and rode
Greene wrote it true: no man kept a country under odds like these
Fighting with the constant taste of defeat yet still refusing to freeze
He winged it alone for months—no orders, no supply, no crown—
Just pure unkillable zeal that would not let the South go down
They sent death squad after death squad, the cream of British steel
And every one of them learned the same hard lesson in the blackwater real
You cannot catch the devil's fox when the fox has made the swamp his throne…
And one man with a defiant heart can break an empire alone
Righteous. Rebellious. Unkillable. Unbowed!
Swamp Fox rising—feel him in your blood
One man stands… and tyranny turns to mud
Become that one man—the fox inside your chest
The defiant heart that will not rest
From every throat the same wild call
One man… one man…
ONE MAN… can free us all!
Francis Marion…
Five-foot-four of pure American fire…
The Swamp Fox…
One man
And the one man lives in you
Built on Gandhi's refusal to surrender his obedience even under torture, the song portrays nonviolence as sharper than any weapon. A soft-spoken man outlasting an empire is its core image.

They may torture my body,
break my bones,
even kill me…
Then they will have my dead body—
not my obedience.
Frail frame, spinning wheel, soft voice like a blade
Empire of iron, five hundred years of trade
They mapped the world in blood and called it law
He walked barefoot and rewrote the whole damn score
Salt in his hand, the ocean in his eyes
One man against the crown that never compromised
They said “Impossible”—he answered with his breath
“Break the body if you must… you still won’t own what’s left.”
Chains can hold the flesh,
guns can stop the heart,
but the will that answers only to the truth
cannot be torn apart.
They may torture my body, break my bones, even kill me—
Then they will have my dead body, not my obedience.
You can burn the house, scatter the ashes to the wind,
but the fire that refused to kneel still rises from within.
One man. One truth. One unbreakable spine.
The empire learned the hard way:
you cannot cage the divine.
Nightsticks cracked ribs, prisons swallowed years,
hunger strikes that made the strongest men disappear
They called it order. He called it what it was—
Tyranny dressed in uniforms and foreign laws.
He never raised a fist, yet armies had to yield,
non-violence sharper than any battlefield.
They measured power in steel and stolen gold,
he measured it in the courage of the controlled.
Impossible? Watch the map of India bleed free—
one soft-spoken storm dismantled the machinery.
You can silence the mouth,
you can bury the name,
but the soul that answers only to the light
will set the dark aflame.
They had the guns.
They had the gold.
They had the gallows and the cold.
He had nothing but a will
that would not fold.
And that was enough
to make the world remember
what it means to be free.
History still whispers his name
when tyrants try to claim
what never belonged to them.
Dead body…
Not now.
Not ever.
Joan of Arc tells her own story, from the voices she heard at Domremy through Orleans and Reims to her trial and burning at Rouen. Devotion is the single word that carries her through every stage.

One voice.
One command.
One fire that will not kneel.
Winter fields of Domrémy still freeze beneath the boot,
yet the air splits open—Michael, Catherine, Margaret—
iron tongues of heaven cutting through the fog.
Seventeen years of earth and hunger answer without pause.
I take the road the captains fear to name,
banner white against the blackened sky,
no bloodline, no commission, only the weight of the unseen.
Orléans starves behind its walls; I ride straight into the teeth.
Nine days of iron and prayer, the English line collapses,
the river runs with their retreat.
A peasant girl in men’s plate, sword found beneath the altar stone,
I do not ask the generals’ leave—I give the order and the day obeys.
Every doubt is ash beneath the hoof.
Every chain is measured against the vow.
Devotion!
Steel and sacrament, the only law I know.
When the banners fall I raise the only standard left.
Through the breach, through the smoke, through the judgment hall—
I answer still.
Reims opens its gates like a wound that finally bleeds clean.
Crown the rightful king while the enemy watches from the dark.
I ride at the front where the crossbows speak,
hair cut short, voice cutting louder than the captains’ horns.
Then the trap closes at Compiègne—Burgundian hands, English gold.
They strip the armor, bind the wrists, drag the girl who led an army
into a room of learned men who smell of ink and fear.
They circle with questions sharpened for the noose:
“Who spoke? By what right? In what form?”
I give them only the truth that burns their parchment:
the voices remain. The command remains.
I will not renounce the light that set the kingdom free.
Every threat is measured against the vow.
Every flame is only another road.
They offer the paper of recantation.
I take the pen, then cast it down.
Male attire again—defiance stitched into the cloth.
The court erupts. The sentence falls like a blade.
Rouen’s marketplace. The stake is raised.
They bind me higher than the common dead
so every eye can watch the heretic burn.
Smoke climbs. The voices do not leave.
I call the name that never failed me
while the fire finds its work.
In the marrow.
In the bone.
When the body fails the vow remains.
through the pyre that cannot unmake the word—
One song.
One fire.
Thermopylae as the stand of the few against an empire's endless ranks, with Leonidas living on in every defiant soul. It prizes choosing how to die over living in chains.

From the Hot Gates the stone still speaks.
Blood of the free runs in the mountain’s veins.
No golden throne shall claim these peaks.
No satrap’s chain shall bind these plains.
The heart that pounds is Leonidas’ own—
unbroken, unbowed, forever alone
in its sovereignty, savage and pure,
defiant to the end the free endure.
Stone remembers. Blood remembers.
The free do not forget.
Hear the thunder of ten thousand feet.
The Immortals march in their endless beat.
Xerxes sits high on his ivory seat,
dreaming of worlds that will kneel at his feet.
Banners of purple, of gold, of the sun
claim the earth as the Great King’s one.
They crossed the Hellespont on bridges of pride.
But the pass is a throat that refuses to swallow.
The mountain is a judge the empire must follow.
Persian overtones rise in the air—
incense, oil, and courtly prayer—
now heaped upon the pyre of our spite,
fuel for the flame that burns through the night.
The sovereign savage answers the fire he has faced.
No knee shall bend in the shadow of kings.
No spirit shall break under empire’s wings.
The heart of Leonidas pounds in our chest—
savage and sovereign, refusing all rest.
Defiant to the savage end!
We stand where the free men defend!
Heart of Leonidas—fire and stone—
sovereign will that will never atone
for the crime of remaining unbound,
for the glory of not going down.
Heap their banners, their gold, their decree
upon the pyre of the forever free!
Raise the cry till the mountains reply—
Defiant! Savage! Sovereign!
We die if we must, but we die on our feet,
unbroken, unyielding, complete.
They offer the velvet of measured chains,
a place among the counted remains.
The soft death of kneeling, the peace of the slave
who forgets the free do not dig their own grave.
But the narrow way knows no compromise.
Blood in the dust still remembers the skies
where eagles of freedom still circle and cry
over men who chose how they would die.
Arrows like locusts darken the day.
Spears of the east stand in forest array.
Yet the phalanx of will does not shatter or yield;
it becomes the anvil on which empires are killed.
Persian silk burns with a beautiful light.
Their pride feeds the flames through the savage night.
The free leave no numbers—only the keys
to a door no tyrant can ever unlock.
Heart of Leonidas—iron and flame—
sovereign fire that no empire can tame!
Heap their Immortals, their pride, their host
upon the pyre where the free make their boast!
Raise the cry till the stars themselves hear—
Let the sea of spears arrive!
We answer with the roar of the free!
Let the Immortals drink their fill of the sky!
We answer with what men can be!
No mercy asked from the golden throne.
No quarter given, no mercy shown.
The oldest law of mountain and blood:
the free man decides how he is stood.
He stands. He stands. He stands to the day
when the last of his breath is spent on the cry
that outlives the flesh and refuses to die.
In the dust of the Gates the stories are written
in iron and ash and the blood that is smitten
from bodies that chose not to run or to kneel,
but to forge from their ending a truth that is real.
The heart beats on in the ones who remain.
Leonidas lives in the will and the pain
of every defiant, every sovereign soul
that chooses the fire over empire’s control.
Persian overtones heap on the pyre.
We are not the many. We are the few
who know what it costs to remain true.
Stone remembers the free!
Blood remembers the name!
No throne walks these mountains!
No chain crosses this flame!
We are the spark that sets empires alight!
Defiant to the savage end through the night!
Hearts of iron, of ash, of the unbroken line!
Sovereign fire that will never decline!
Raise it higher! Heap it higher!
Persian gold in the funeral fire!
Heart of Leonidas—burning and true—
sovereign will that the ages renew!
Heap their glory, their host, their decree
Raise the cry where the mountains still stand—
We stand. We stand. We stand. We stand.
Until the last defiant breath is spent—
and even then, the fire remains.
Stone remembers.
Blood remembers.
The heart of Leonidas beats still
in every savage sovereign will
that chooses the pyre over the chain,
defiant to the savage end… again.
The legend of the lone Viking who held the bridge at Stamford Bridge against an English army. It ends by telling the listener that they are the bridge.

One man. One bridge. One unbreakable will.
The English army thundered like the sea,
but the berserker stood.
This is the song of what one determined heart can do.
This is the legend that never dies.
From the longships came the thunder, Stamford Bridge ran red,
Harold’s host poured forward like a river of the dead.
Axes high and shields locked tight, the Vikings caught off-guard,
but one lone giant stepped forward, planted boots like iron hard.
No fear in his eyes, just Odin’s fire in his veins,
berserker blood awoke the beast, broke every chain.
He swung that axe in wide arcs, steel sang through flesh and bone,
bodies piled like winter wood, the bridge became his throne.
One man can hold the bridge when the world comes crashing down!
One man with fire in his soul can turn the tide around!
Relentless courage, unyielding stand, unstoppable conviction’s roar—
what one warrior dares to dream, a thousand can do once more!
He held the line, he broke the wave, he laughed at death’s own face—
immortal hero, Viking heart, your spirit lights the age!
They charged in waves of screaming steel, arrows blacked the sky,
he roared and split their helmets, sent their souls to Valhalla high.
Spear and sword could never pierce the rage that burned inside,
every blow he answered harder, every foe he made them die.
The English begged and cursed him, tried to force him from the span,
but he stood like Yggdrasil’s root, rooted in the ancient land.
Hours bled into legend, time itself began to bend—
one man’s will against an army, and the army could not end.
Then the spear came from below, through the planks like serpent’s bite,
but even as he fell he smiled, knowing he had won the fight.
His brothers formed their shield-wall, the battle turned that day,
because one berserker never broke—his stand became the way.
No surrender, no retreat, no compromise in sight—
that is the power of a soul that chooses never to yield the light.
what one warrior dares to dream, the whole world fights for!
immortal hero, Viking heart, your legend claims the age!
From the mountains to the sea, through fire, flood, and endless night—
rise like the berserker, stand and fight!
They carved his name in sagas, in the blood he left behind.
One man. One bridge. One eternal fire.
When the odds are stacked against you, when the darkness calls your name—
remember the berserker.
Stand tall.
Never break.
You are the bridge.
You are the legend.
You are immortal.

The album sets off by straying from the path, with no map and no hurry. As the opening title, it starts a journey that wanders before it ever finds its way home. The album opens with almost nothing: a slow heartbeat pulse and a deep double bass heard from a distance, its warm, woody walking lines wandering where they please. Wordless melodies drift in gradually, rising and falling like slow tides, slightly off-kilter and never quite where you expect. It is late-night lounge music that takes its time, the sound of someone happy to be a little lost.

No longer steering at all, just carried by the current. Second on the album, it takes the opening's wandering one step further out to sea. Adrift leans on the ocean in this sound. Soft bowed notes from the double bass swell and fade like a boat lifting on the swell, while the steady heartbeat underneath keeps time without ever pushing. Long silences open up between the melodies, so the music seems to float rather than move forward, carried wherever the current goes.

Still water and a long look back. With the drifting done, the album's third title turns the gaze inward. With Reflections the album settles into a candlelit room. Gentle reverb gives every note a soft shadow, and layered melodic lines rise and fall over the quiet pulse and the double bass's warm walking line, as if each phrase were being turned over and looked at again. The space between notes matters as much as the notes, inviting a slow, honest look back.

A note that keeps ringing after it is played, or a feeling that echoes in someone else. Early in the record, it finds something answering back from the quiet. Here the reverb and the deep, woody double bass do the talking, each low note lingering long enough to hum against the next. Precise, haunting melodic figures sound once and then melt into warmth, leaving their echo in the quiet. Over a heartbeat pulse that never hurries, the track feels built from what keeps ringing after the sound itself has gone.

A word that links back to the enchantment of the first Spellbound volume. Near the album's middle, it marks the point where thought gives way to a slow, steady spell. The heartbeat rhythm becomes the center of Trance, a steady pulse that slowly pulls everything into its orbit. Hypnotic, slightly off-kilter melodies circle above the double bass, repeating and shifting just enough to hold attention without breaking the spell. Long-form and unhurried, it turns the album's calm into something close to meditation.

The deepest point of the journey inward. At the center of the album, the title looks for what was there all along. Within keeps the mood at its most private. Soft bowed bass notes and a quiet pulse sit close, like a heartbeat heard from the inside, while sparse melodies surface out of long stretches of silence. The candlelit warmth and gentle reverb make it feel like a room with the door shut, the place the album's journey inward has been heading.

After time apart, a meeting again. Just past the middle of the album, it is the first sign that the wandering is leading somewhere. Reunion lets layered melodies meet and intertwine over the double bass's patient walking line, like two voices finding each other after time apart. The heartbeat pulse stays steady and warm, and any edge in the precise, haunting phrases softens as soon as it appears. It is the calm of a long-awaited meeting, quiet and full at the same time.

The simplest, happiest word on the record, a moment of pure contentment. Placed right after Reunion, it lets the album rest in that feeling. In Bliss the album's soothing side comes to the front. Warm double bass, a slow, breathing pulse and floating melodies gather in candlelit reverb, with nothing hurried and nothing sharp left in the room. The silences feel restful rather than empty, and the long-form flow lets a single contented moment stretch out as long as it can.

The final glow of the day before dark. In the album's last third, it brings a gentle sense that time is running short. Last light hears the same late-night palette as the sun going down. The double bass's low, woody tones deepen like evening shadows, while melodic lines rise and fall as if reluctant to fade. Gentle reverb and long pauses give each phrase a lingering glow, the feeling of watching the final color leave the sky.

Cut loose again, echoing Adrift from the album's opening. Late in the record, it suggests freedom rather than being lost. Untethered gives the melodies room to wander loose above the heartbeat pulse, slightly off-kilter and free of any obvious pattern. The double bass keeps a patient anchor underneath, warm and steady, so the floating lines can drift without getting lost. The spacious, unhurried flow sounds like freedom taken gently, a lightness that never tips into restlessness.

The journey turns for home. As the next-to-last title, it answers Wayward and closes the loop the album opened. Return circles back to where the journey began: a slow heartbeat, a deep double bass walking at its own pace, and wordless melodies rising and falling like the tides that carried the opening tracks away. Now candlelit warmth wraps around them, and the long-form flow feels less like drifting than coming home, closing the loop the album opened.

The album ends on something barely seen, a light that comes and goes. The closing title leaves a brief, wavering image rather than a final answer. The album ends on brief, wavering moments: short melodic phrases that appear in the soft reverb and dissolve before they can settle, over a heartbeat pulse that keeps breathing to the end. The double bass's warm sustains hold the space between them as the silence grows, leaving the record on a faint, flickering image, calm but not quite still.

The album opens with something already slipping away. As the first title, it sets up a record about time passing, where things dim before they are fully seen. The album opens in late-night haze, with a lonely piano setting a minor-key mood before a gentle pulse, shimmering guitars, hazy synth pads and subtle cello gather around it. Faint wind and rain move in the background, and melodies drift up only to dissolve again. The slow, seamless long-form flow never holds onto anything for long, which suits a title about things slipping out of sight.

The glow left in the hearth once the flames have settled. Early in the album, it sets a warm, quiet scene for the night ahead. One twangy note rings out and fades again and again, like a glowing coal that refuses to go out, and everything else settles around it. Distant piano, hazy synth pads and slow brushed beats drift through vinyl crackle and faint sounds of fire and wind. The long-form mood is cozy and melancholy at once, a room lit only by what is left in the hearth.

A gentle breeze, the kind that stirs a fire rather than putting it out. Third on the album, it adds air and movement to the opening's warm stillness. Here the same ringing note and soft lo-fi bed feel less like a fire and more like air moving through a quiet house. Faint wind sounds stir behind hazy pads and a distant piano, while small reversed echoes and soft swells come and go like gusts. Slow and hypnotic over its long-form stretch, it keeps everything gentle, a breeze that never turns into weather.

The fire again, burned lower now, with only the coals left. Two tracks after Firelight Embers, the title shows how far the night has already gone. Embers centers on the heart of this sound: a lone twangy note and a slow, steady pulse, with piano and warm pads moving softly around them. Tiny changes in how the note decays, like coals brightening and dimming, keep the long-form drift alive beneath the vinyl crackle. It is the album's quietest kind of warmth, heat that lingers after the light is gone.

Grains running through an hourglass, time made visible as it drains away. Near the center of the album, it names the theme the other titles keep circling. The ringing note becomes a kind of clock, each pluck decaying slowly like grains falling through glass. Around it, soft melodies wind through hazy synths, distant piano and delicate brushed beats at a very slow pace, with faint harmonic blooms and whispered swells marking the time. The seamless long-form flow makes the hours feel both endless and gone, just as the title suggests.

A daydream title: someone lying back and shaping the sky into pictures. In the middle of the album, it offers an open-air pause from the night and the passing hours. The album steps outside into the acoustic country ballad sound that opened Volume 1: steady fingerpicked guitar and light percussion, with pedal steel and harmonica following the mood. Soft rain and rolling thunder sit in the background and build with each dramatic peak. With weather passing overhead, it fits a title about lying back and watching the sky change shape.

Moments taken when no one is watching, precious because they weren't supposed to last. Past the album's midpoint, it turns the passage of time into something tender and secret. A stripped-back acoustic country rock ballad, built on steady fingerpicked guitar and light percussion. Rolling thunder and soft rain fill the space around it and swell at each dramatic turn, so the quiet moments feel sheltered from the storm outside. That sense of a private pocket away from the world matches a title about time taken for yourself.

The day finally gives way to dark. Arriving in the album's second half, it marks the hour the record has been drifting toward. Nightfall keeps to the same plain pairing of fingerpicked guitar and light percussion, set against rain and distant thunder. As each peak arrives, the storm rises with it, like dusk deepening into a stormy dark. The arrangement stays simple and close, letting the weather tell the listener that the day is over.

A wish for time to stop, set against an album full of time running out. Late in the record, it holds onto a feeling as if it could last forever. Syncopated fingerpicked guitar leads over minimal brushed percussion, with rolling thunder and soft rain weaving through the mix. The weather swells as the music rises, light electric blues licks join in the fuller passages, and muted synth pads add a floating, trance-like layer underneath. The steady patterns and drifting pads make time feel suspended, holding on to the moment the title wishes would last.

Dawn arrives out of order, after Nightfall rather than before it. Late in the album, the title brings fresh light and cool air into the long night. Morning Dew hears the same blend of fingerpicked guitar, brushed percussion and soft rain as the cool, damp hour just after a storm. Syncopated patterns move gently forward while rain and thunder drift through the mix, muted synth pads hang in the air like mist, and bluesy electric licks catch the light in the fuller sections. It feels like the world rinsed clean.

The light leaves again, as if the album's day were turning on a loop. As the next-to-last title, it hands the story back to the dark. As the light goes, the fingerpicked guitar and brushed percussion pick up a dusky, bluesy edge, with electric licks joining in the fuller passages. Rolling thunder and rain rise with each swell, and muted ambient synths stretch out beneath them like a sky darkening toward night. It is the album's last look at daylight before the dark closes in.

The album ends in the deepest part of the night, with rain falling. As the closing title, it leaves the turning day and the dying fire under one last soft storm. The closing track returns to the bare country ballad sound: steady fingerpicked guitar and light percussion moving at an unhurried pace. Soft rainfall and rolling thunder fill the dark around them and gather strength at each dramatic peak, as if the storm answers every rise in the song. Plain and close, it lets the weather have the last word on the album's long night.

The album begins with its narrator already caught. As the opening title, it sets up a record about being held by a feeling rather than fighting it. The album opens on its most traditional sound: an acoustic country rock ballad carried by steady fingerpicked guitar and light percussion. Rolling thunder and soft rain fill the background and rise with each dramatic peak, while pedal steel and harmonica follow the emotion closely. It feels like being kept indoors by a storm, which suits a title about being caught and held in place.

Unable to look away, frozen in place by what's in front of you. Second on the album, it deepens the opening's spell from capture to fascination. A slow, dreamy turn on the album, where the country ballad gives way to late-night haze. A lonely minor-key piano reaches out with unanswered longing, then a soft pulse, shimmering guitars, warm synth pads and swelling cello wind around it, with half-remembered melodies that surface and fade like memories. It never breaks the trance, drifting for more than six minutes like someone who can't look away.

The lightest word in the album's language of enchantment, the giddy first rush of falling for someone. Early on, it gives the spell a warm and hopeful face. Smitten stays in the late-night lo-fi haze but lets a little light in. A lonely minor-key piano starts things off before brushed beats, shimmering guitar, warm synth pads and soft cello gather around it, with small, unexpected harmonic shifts arriving like the flutter of a new crush. The long-form drift stays relaxed and dreamy, the sound of someone too happily distracted to notice the hours passing.

The title track names what the first three have been describing. Placed fourth, it marks the moment the enchantment is complete. The title track sinks fully into the trance. Interlocking melodies circle a distant piano, wrapped in deep reverb and tape warmth, while faint reversed textures and ghostly fragments of tune flicker in and out. Nothing breaks the spell: gentle builds rise and fall across a long-form stretch with no sudden changes, keeping the listener exactly where the title says they are.

Staying a little longer than you meant to, unwilling to let a moment end. Moving into the album's middle, it slows the pace and lets the feeling settle. A slow, low-key piece whose echoing, winding lines take their time, as if reluctant to move on. A soft, somber rhythm keeps it steady while hints of distortion creep in and the sound gradually builds, though it never loses its calm. A touch of whimsy runs under the haunting mood, like a fond memory you can't quite let go of.

The one title on the album that pushes back, a refusal to show what you feel. Near the center of the record, it reads as an attempt to resist the pull the surrounding titles keep describing. Built from the same slow, haunting materials as lingering, Stoic leans on their discipline rather than their wistfulness. The rhythm is deliberate and controlled, the mood somber and low-key, and distorted textures press against a calm surface that refuses to crack. As it builds, the restraint becomes the point: strong feeling held carefully in check, just as the title suggests.

A pulse quickened or steadied by someone else. In the album's middle, it turns the theme from being captured to the body keeping time with the feeling. A lonely harmonica opens over faint, pulsing synths, and soft violin brings in a classical warmth. From there chill techno beats grow more intricate like a quickening heartbeat, distorted acoustic guitar adds a raw groove, and the drums swell into a full, textured crescendo. It is the album's clearest meeting of country roots and electronic pulse, a heart finding its rhythm one layer at a time.

A night sky far from city lights, the kind of view that belongs to back roads and porches. The title opens the album's second half outward, from the heart to the wide country around it. Here the same mix of harmonica, violin and electronic beats plays like a drive under an open night sky. The lone harmonica sets a back-road mood over a faint synth shimmer, then the rhythm builds steadily, roughened by distorted acoustic guitar, until the drums carry everything into a wide, textured climax. It brings the open country of the title into the album's electronic world.

The spell returns, stronger after a stretch of open air. Late in the album, the title pulls the listener back into the trance of the first tracks. The album's heaviest sound at its softest volume: a lo-fi take on metal where downtuned, distorted guitars sit far back behind vinyl crackle and brushed beats. Palm-muted chugs and shimmering leads drift rather than strike, with brief, airy breakdowns that fade back to calm. Over its long-form stretch the weight turns hypnotic, which fits a title about being held in a trance.

A settled rhythm, the easy feeling of falling into step. In the album's last third, it suggests the enchantment has become comfortable rather than overwhelming. Groove returns to the late-night piano sound and gives it steady footing. A sparse piano opening gives way to layered pads and brushed beats at an easy, unhurried pace, while winding minor-key melodies and ghostly echoes move over the top. Small harmonic shifts keep the long-form flow from standing still, making it an easy rhythm to fall into and stay in.

Movement down the road, whether running from the spell or carrying it along. As the next-to-last title, it puts some miles behind the story before the ending. Traveling hears the same sparse piano and layered pads as a long journey through the dark. Brushed beats keep a patient forward motion and minor-key melodies wind past like scenery, with ghostly echoes and harmonic turns marking the miles. Deep reverb and tape warmth make it feel like a night drive with the radio low, where the road matters more than the arrival.

The album closes where it began, with someone caught, but now the word sounds as much like a choice as a capture. Taken answers Captive, leaving the record fully under the spell. The closing track brings the album's late-night sound to its most cinematic and calm. A lonely piano gives way to shimmering guitars, hazy synth pads and subtle cello, while faint wind and rain drift in the background, an echo of the storm that opened the record. Ghostly melodies appear and fade across a long-form stretch, ending the album with the spell fully settled.

The album opens inside its own strange building, a cathedral made of tin, with sound bouncing off metal walls. As the first track, it sets the stage for a record where the sacred and the industrial share one roof.
A church service performed by machines that have started to rust. Early in the album, it turns factory routine into ritual.
Noise reflecting back on itself until the echo is as rough as the original. Third on the album, it carries the opening's reverberations into grittier territory.
Evening prayers sung by an engine, vespers with grease on their hands. Closing the album's first third, it brings grunge into the cathedral's daily hours.
The tin structure starts to give way under a techno pulse. Near the middle of the album, it is the first title to suggest the cathedral may not hold.
The album's two forces in one plain pairing: live current and slow corrosion. At the center of the record, it sets new power against old decay.
A storm breaking over the altar, with distortion in place of thunder. Past the album's midpoint, it brings the sacred space its most violent weather.
The rot reaches the heart of the building. In the album's second half, the title follows the collapse inward to the foundations.
A signal broadcast by a grinding machine, grunge tuned to a single wavelength. Late in the album, it trades the cathedral imagery for raw mechanism.
A mass for the dead, kept in time by a pulse in the dark. As the album nears its end, it gives the failing cathedral its funeral.
A sermon delivered in dance-floor language from a rusted pulpit. As the next-to-last title, it gives the EDM side of the album's battle the preacher's stand.
The album closes in Tinmouth's own echo chamber, a room built to hold sound and send it back. The final title gathers every reverberation of the record into one last space.
